idiom_name: flow controller + command registry + decision rules + view resolver
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: one object or module owns the flow. It keeps the conversation's progress in an application context (session-scoped), exposes a single entry point that receives an event - a submitted form, a chosen menu item, a domain callback - and returns the pair (command to run, view to show next). Commands are represented as small objects or functions over the model so the same unit of work is callable from several steps, and views are referenced by abstract names that a resolver outside the controller turns into pages. The decisions themselves are data: a transition table, guard predicates or a state machine, never if-chains inside the views. Keep the controller free of the UI machinery (read and write the session through an abstraction, never HttpServletRequest directly). The controller is injected into page controllers and presenters so the same flow can be driven from different front ends. One Application Controller per related group of views is the right granularity; a single global controller for a large app is an anti-pattern.
code_sketch:
controller = FlowController(flow_rules)            # states + events + guards
ctx = context_from(request)                      # session/progress, no HTTP inside
cmd, view = controller.handle(ctx, event_from(request))
if cmd: cmd.run(ctx.model)                       # the unit of work, not domain logic
render(view, ctx.model)                           # resolver picks the real template
pitfalls: Letting the controller grow domain logic: once it also computes prices or validates business rules, the flow cannot be changed without touching behaviour - keep it to decisions and delegate the work.
Sharing mutable controller state across sessions; the flow definition may be shared, but the progress belongs to the conversation.
Returning a rendered response from the controller instead of a decision, which welds the flow to one presentation technology and makes it untestable without a rendering stack.
Hard-coding the view class or template path inside the controller instead of returning a view id; this breaks multiple-front-end scenarios and complicates testing.
Storing the current step as a bare integer in the session with no versioning: a code redeploy that changes the step numbering silently breaks in-progress conversations.
Not expiring abandoned flows: a wizard started but never finished leaves session data orphaned; implement a time-to-live and a cleanup job.
Making the Application Controller a static class: it prevents dependency injection, makes testing require global state, and becomes a service-locator anti-pattern with hidden dependencies.
Allowing views to redirect directly to other views without going through the controller ('flow drift'), silently recreating the duplication the pattern was meant to remove.
Building a single global Application Controller for a large application: unrelated flows accumulate in one place, creating a change bottleneck where modifying one wizard risks breaking another.
Encoding transition rules as if/else chains inside the controller rather than as data: every rule change requires code changes and full regression testing instead of a simple table update.
Skipping illegal-transition tests: only testing happy paths means invalid events at a given state silently produce wrong views, and the flow can enter undefined states under adversarial input.
Leaking conversation state into URLs or hidden form fields without server-side validation: an attacker can modify the step id to skip mandatory screens, bypassing guards and validation gates.

Allowing multiple open tabs or windows to share the same session-scoped conversation state: interleaved transitions corrupt the flow state without a concurrency guard (optimistic lock or sequence number).

Re-deploying with a changed flow definition while active conversations use the old schema: without a migration path, users resuming a paused wizard encounter type errors or land on steps that no longer exist.

Adding step-specific side effects inside the controller rather than in commands: the controller becomes a macro for a dozen unrelated if-blocks, and no flow participant can predict what will run on a given transition.

Putting URL dispatch or page rendering into this controller makes it a Front Controller or Page Controller with a misleading name, so unrelated requests couple to the flow; keep transport routing and per-screen rendering outside and return an abstract view decision.

Using an Intercepting Filter to choose the next wizard step makes branches depend on request wrapping order and loses conversation ownership; reserve filters or middleware for cross-cutting pre/post work and let the Application Controller evaluate state transitions.

Wrong move: keeping the authoritative process state in the web-tier controller while a domain workflow engine or process manager also tracks it -> the two copies diverge after a compensating action, admin override or expiry -> instead let the domain process own the state and reduce the Application Controller to dispatching events to it and rendering its answers.

Wrong move: one monolithic state machine for every journey because the framework wires a single flow -> unrelated teams serialise on the same flow definition and a checkout edit regresses onboarding -> instead scope one flow per journey with explicit entry and exit points and compose them, as ADF bounded task flows and Spring Web Flow subflows do.

Wrong move: declaring a transition table but letting events with no matching case fall through to a default view -> a typo or missing guard silently skips a mandatory step under adversarial input -> instead make every unmatched state/event pair a typed error and test the full state x event matrix including the illegal cells.

Letting each page controller redirect directly to the next page makes conditional rules diverge and flow tests miss paths; send an application event to the controller and resolve one next-view decision there.
